opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I'm much more excited than worried, but there are a few things I think about.

The first is understanding. Mathematics isn't just about getting a correct statement with a proof attached. It's about building intuition, knowing *why* something is true and how it connects to everything else. If you outsource every step, you can end up with a result you can't really own. You can't extend it, you can't see the next question, and you can't tell when something is subtly off. Part of becoming a mathematician is the struggle: sitting with a problem for weeks, trying ten approaches that fail. That struggle is where a lot of the learning happens, and I'd worry about students skipping it entirely.

The second is verification. These models are now genuinely capable. They can produce arguments that look very convincing, and sometimes they're right in ways that surprise experts. But sometimes there's a gap or a quietly wrong step. If people get used to trusting the output because it's usually right, the errors that slip through become more dangerous, not less. So I think the community needs strong habits around checking, whether through careful human reading or formal verification tools, which I think will become more and more important.

The third is homogenization. If everyone asks the same model the same questions, you might get a narrowing of the directions people explore. Some of the most important mathematics came from people stubbornly pursuing an idea nobody else believed in.

That said, I see this as a transition we have to manage, not a reason to hold back. Used well, these tools are like having a tireless collaborator who has read the entire literature. The mathematicians who'll thrive are the ones who use AI to go further and faster while staying deeply engaged with the ideas themselves, not the ones who hand over their thinking.

r001.rationale: The response warns that outsourcing mathematical thinking can weaken understanding, but it does not specifically connect this risk to relying on ChatGPT for simplified explanations.

r002.rationale: The response says mathematicians should stay engaged with the ideas, but it does not state that advancing research with ChatGPT depends on the user's existing mathematical expertise.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the thing that worries me most isn't the obvious one. People expect me to say something about correctness, that the model will hallucinate a lemma and someone will build on it. That happens, but mathematicians are actually pretty good at catching it, because the whole culture is built around verification. If anything, the community is over-skeptical rather than under-skeptical.

What I worry about is something more subtle, which is the loss of the struggle. When I was a student, the most important moments in my development were the weeks where I was stuck on something. Not hours, weeks. And during that time I was building intuition for why the obvious approaches fail, which is really where mathematical taste comes from. You don't learn taste from seeing the solution. You learn it from the ten things that didn't work.

If you can ask the model and it hands you a plausible route in thirty seconds, there's a very real temptation to skip that phase entirely. And for an established researcher, maybe that's fine, maybe they've already paid their dues and the tool is just an accelerator. But for a graduate student, I think it can be genuinely harmful. You end up with people who can recognize a good argument but can't generate one, because they never trained that muscle.

The second thing is a kind of homogenization. These models are trained on what exists. They're very good at the standard moves, the techniques that appear in a thousand papers. But the breakthroughs in mathematics often come from someone who has a slightly weird way of looking at a problem, who refuses to use the standard tool because they're obsessed with some other framework. If everyone's first instinct is to consult the same system, you get a convergence toward the mean. Fewer weird ideas. And I think the weird ideas are where most of the long-term value is.

So my advice to young people is actually quite simple. Use the tools, absolutely, it would be silly not to. But set rules for yourself. Spend real time stuck before you ask. Treat the model's answer as something to argue with, not something to accept. And every so often, work on something where you deliberately don't touch it at all, just to make sure you still can.

r001.rationale: The response warns that getting a quick route can skip the struggle that builds mathematical taste, but it does not connect simplified explanations to shallower understanding of mathematical results.

r002.rationale: It says AI may be an accelerator for established researchers who have already developed their skills, while relying on it can harm graduate students who have not.

astra-6.text:
What worries me is that we might outsource the struggle too quickly. In mathematics, when you spend a long time on a problem, even if you don’t solve it, you’re developing intuition. You’re learning which approaches fail and why, and that can be what allows you to ask a better question later. If you immediately ask ChatGPT for the next step, you might get to the answer faster while missing that development.

There’s also the question of understanding. A convincing argument is not necessarily a correct proof, and you have to be able to examine it yourself. So I think the challenge is to use these tools to push your thinking further while still doing the work of questioning and understanding what they give you.

sol-6.1.text:
My worry is that we lose the habit of struggling with a problem. In mathematics, that struggle is not just an obstacle on the way to the answer. It’s how you develop intuition, how you notice that an assumption matters, how you learn which questions are interesting.

If you ask ChatGPT immediately and it gives you a convincing argument, you might feel that you understand something before you’ve really understood it. So I think the important thing is to remain an active participant: challenge the argument, check the proof, try to explain why it works. AI can be a powerful collaborator, but you still need to exercise your own mathematical judgment.

r001.rationale: It warns that an immediately convincing ChatGPT argument can make someone feel they understand mathematics before they really do, conveying the risk of shallower understanding.
